text: Curry painted rural life in his home state of Kansas. He was hailed as one of the three great painters of American Regionalism of the first half of the twentieth century, along with Thomas Hart Benton and Grant Wood. His work was varied, including paintings, book illustrations, prints and posters. He was Kansas's best-known painter, but Kansans did not like his works, because they felt he did not portray the state positively. The Line Storm is among his pictures.

Madrazo began his studies at the Real Academia de Bellas Artes de San Fernando with Gregorio Ferro, a student of Anton Raphael Mengs. After 1803 he studied in Paris with Jacques-Louis David, and on David's advice he applied for a government stipend to study in Rome. In 1806 he went to Rome. He was one of the primary exponents of the Neoclassical style in Spain, and the patriarch of a family of artists that included his sons Federico and Luis and his grandsons Raimundo and Ricardo.

Artist, writer, mercenary and Reformed politician, Niklaus Manuel came from Bern. His father was most likely Emanuel Aleman, a pharmacist whose own father had come from Chieri in Piedmont. He took his father's given name, Manuel, as his surname and added Deutsch, the German equivalent of Alleman. He signed his works with the initials NMD. Mercenary Beggar is among his works.

Ozanne was schooled from 1750 at the Ecole des Gardes de la Marine and in Paris, where he was a pupil of Duhamel du Monceau. He returned to Brest in 1764 as drawing professor at the naval academy. He took part in scientific expeditions, in 1776 on the Boussole. When the American war of independence began, he served on the Languedoc and the Vautour. His brother Nicolas was an artist too.

Cochin the Elder painted like his father until he was twenty-two, when he gave up painting and devoted himself entirely to engraving. In 1731 he became an Academician, and for his reception he engraved portraits of Jacques Sarrazin and Eustache Le Sueur. Then he turned to the fancy subjects of Watteau, Lancret and Chardin, and made several works after them. He married the engraver Louise-Magdeleine Horthemels.

Peyron came from a wealthy family in Aix-en-Provence and studied law until his father died in 1765. He then enrolled at the drawing school in Aix, where the history painter Michel-François Dandré-Bardon taught him. In 1767 he moved to Paris and entered the atelier of the Rococo painter Louis Jean François Lagrenée. His The Death of Socrates in Prison dates from 1786.

The Master of Alkmaar gets his name from a series of panel paintings of the Seven Works of Mercy, made in 1504 for the church of Saint Lawrence in Alkmaar and now in the Rijksmuseum. The paintings bear the stamp of Geertgen tot Sint Jans. They are done in bright colours, and the figures are drawn in an exaggeratedly caricatured manner. One proposal identifies him with Cornelis Buys I, the brother of Jacob Cornelisz van Oostsanen.

Broders is best known for travel posters promoting tourism in France, typically fashionable beaches on the Côte d'Azur and skiing resorts in the French Alps. His illustrations are distinctive for simple lines and bold, flat areas of colour, with a noticeable graphical perspective that puts mountains and seascapes in the background. His people are active, elongated figures wearing elegant, contemporary clothes. He was born and died in Paris.

Adam-Salomon's father wanted him to become a merchant. After a brief career as a modeler at the Jacob Petit pottery factory in Fontainebleau, he received a scholarship to study sculpture in Paris. He also travelled to Switzerland and England to study. His notable sculptures include busts of Victor Cousin and Odilon Barrot. He worked as a photographer as well, and made portraits of Alphonse Karr, Charles Garnier and Émile Augier.

Information about Onofri's early life is scarce. He was born in Rome, but the date is not entirely clear, and estimates run from 1630 to 1650. He is believed to have been one of the few pupils of Gaspard Dughet, a painter of French descent who spent his whole life in Italy. He collaborated with many specialist figure painters of his time. He worked in Rome and Florence as a landscape painter, draughtsman and engraver.

Amsterdam was where Santvoort was born and died. In 1648 he married and had a son named Rembrandt. Though not registered as a pupil of Rembrandt, he is considered a member of Rembrandt's school, making portraits and historical allegories. He was the brother of the landscape painter Pieter Dircksz Santvoort. He married a second time in 1657. His Portrait of Elizabeth Spiegel is among his works.

London was where Devis was born, the nineteenth child of the artist Arthur Devis. His older brother Thomas Anthony was a painter too, and his sister Ellin was a schoolmistress and grammarian. He painted portraits and historical subjects, and he exhibited sixty-five of them at the Royal Academy. Among his more famous works are a depiction of the Death of Nelson and a posthumous portrait of Nelson.

Thayer was known for her floral paintings, and some of her works are at the Smithsonian American Art Museum. The museum credits her with studies for the illustrations in Concealing Coloration in the Animal Kingdom, including studies of caterpillars. Her 1904 study of The Cotton-Tail Rabbit among Dry Grasses and Leaves is in the Brooklyn Museum. She was born in New York City. Her father was Moses S. Beach, and her grandfather was Moses Yale Beach.

Born in Rostock, Cleyn showed such ability as a youth that he was kept in the service of Christian IV of Denmark. In 1611 he painted a half-length portrait of Christian, now in Copenhagen, and made decorative works in Rosenborg castle and elsewhere. There he met Sir Robert Anstruther, then England's ambassador extraordinary to the Danish court. He later lived and worked in England as a painter and as a designer of woven wall hangings.

Born Louis Assez Noël in Quimper, he got his first drawing lessons from his father, a draftsman working on the canal from Nantes to Brest. He later studied at the Académie Charioux in Brest. Then he went to Paris to seek his fortune and came under the influence of his fellow Breton painter Pierre-Julien Gilbert. He painted landscapes and maritime scenes, mainly in Brittany and Normandy. He died in Algiers.

Monziès began to learn painting and etching in Paris in 1871, from Jean-Louis Ernest Meissonier and Isidore Pils, and from the etcher Léon Gaucherel. He won second-class and third-class medals at the Salon. In 1882 he married Eugénie Alphonsine Courtignon, and they had three children. For the last ten years of his life he was curator of the three museums of Le Mans. The Geese of Brother Philippe is among his pictures.

Merian received her artistic training from her stepfather, Jacob Marrel, a student of the still life painter Georg Flegel. She published her first book of natural illustrations in 1675. She was one of the earliest European naturalists to document insects by observing them directly, and her work showed that insects have a life cycle and do not appear by spontaneous generation. Her Caterpillar Book includes the metamorphosis of a small emperor moth on a damson plum.

Gottlieb died at 23, but he is considered one of the most talented students of Jan Matejko. He was one of eleven children in a wealthy Orthodox Jewish family in Drohobycz. Michał Godlewski introduced him to painting in Lemberg. At fifteen he enrolled at the Vienna academy for three years, and in 1873 he went to Kraków to study under Matejko. His Shylock and Jessica is among his pictures.

The son of a dice maker in Antwerp, Simon de Vos started his art studies at twelve with the portrait painter Cornelis de Vos, who was not related to him. He began by making small cabinet pictures of genre scenes, in particular Caravaggesque merry companies. Later he switched to history painting on a larger scale, in a Flemish Baroque style influenced by Rubens and Van Dyck. He was also a draughtsman and an art collector.

Gelton is known for buying paintings in 1658 for the Swedish king Charles X Gustav and for the family of the noble Magnus Gabriel de la Gardie. Little is known of his early life, but he seems to have been trained in The Hague, where he belonged to the Confrerie Pictura. He was influenced by popular Dutch painters, most notably Gerrit Dou and Cornelis van Poelenburgh, and made copies after them. He lived in Stockholm from 1666, and in 1674 he became court painter to King Christian V of Denmark. He died in Copenhagen.

Rogers taught himself to draw. His mother sent a selection of his sketches to a newspaper in Dayton, Ohio, and at fourteen his first cartoons appeared there. He studied at the Worcester Polytechnic Institute and Wittenberg College but never graduated. His career as an illustrator started in 1873, when the Daily Graphic in New York hired him at nineteen. His cartoons for Harper's Weekly include Uncle Sam's New Class in the Art of Self-Government.

Aspertini's complex, eccentric, eclectic style anticipates Mannerism. He came from a Bologna family of painters, including his father Giovanni Antonio and his brother Guido, and studied under Lorenzo Costa and Francesco Francia. He travelled to Rome with his father in 1496 and is briefly documented there again between 1500 and 1503. Then he returned to Bologna. He is considered one of the leading exponents of the Bolognese School of painting.

Stettheimer painted her friends, family and New York experiences in a feminine, theatrical style. She made the first feminist nude self-portrait. She and her sisters hosted a salon that attracted members of the avant-garde. In the mid-1930s she created the stage designs and costumes for Four Saints in Three Acts, the opera by Gertrude Stein and Virgil Thomson. She was also a poet.

Dumont painted portrait miniatures. He was left an orphan young, with five brothers and sisters to support. He studied for a while under Jean Girardet, and then, on the advice of the academician Madame Coster, set up a studio of his own in Lunéville. In 1784 he went to Rome and returned four years later after careful study. In 1788 he was accepted as an Academician and granted an apartment in the Louvre.

About 680 of Gertrud Kauders's artworks were discovered unexpectedly in Prague in 2018, the entire contents of her studio. She was a Czech painter of Jewish descent who disappeared in 1942 and was killed in a Nazi extermination camp. She grew up in Prague's Old Town with her older brother Hans, in a cosmopolitan, secular, German-speaking household. Her parents, Sigmund and Emmy, came from well established, affluent Prague Jewish families, and they encouraged their children to pursue cultural and artistic interests.

A sailor's son from Pargas, Finnberg went to Turku in 1800 to apprentice as a painter, and in 1805 he graduated as a journeyman, with a portrait of a man in red chalk as his graduation work. The next year he left for Stockholm to study at the Royal Swedish Academy of Arts, where Louis Masreliez's recommendation got him straight into the higher courses. He did well. He never officially graduated.

Zille's father had been a blacksmith, then became a watchmaker, goldsmith and inventor of tools. His childhood was troubled, because his father was put in debtors' prison several times and creditors harassed the family. Heinrich was born in Radeburg near Dresden and spent his early years in Potschappel. He worked as an illustrator and caricaturist, and also as a lithographer and photographer. Five Working-Class Children is among his works.

Haarlem was where Van Nickelen was born and died. According to Houbraken he painted church interiors in the manner of Hendrick Cornelisz. van Vliet, and he mentions him in relation to his son, the landscape painter Jan van Nickelen. The RKD says he became a master of the Haarlem Guild of St Luke in 1660 and did well with his church interiors. He lived to a great age and went bankrupt near the end of his life, in 1698.

The older brother of the painter Gerrit, whom he later taught to paint, Job Berckheyde was born in Haarlem. In 1644 he was apprenticed to Jacob Willemszoon de Wet, whose influence shows in his first dated canvas, Christ Preaching to the Children, one of his few biblical scenes. The two brothers later made an extended trip together. Job worked in Haarlem, Amsterdam and The Hague. He also painted the interior of the Church of St Bavo in Haarlem.

Seutter began as an apprentice brewer, but the beer business did not inspire him. He left, moved to Nuremberg and apprenticed as an engraver under the prominent Johann Homann. Sometime in the early eighteenth century he left Homann and set up his own cartographic publishing firm in Augsburg. He struggled in the early years of his independent work. Seutter was born and died in Augsburg.

Jules Renard drew under the name Draner, an anagram of his surname, and he used it on all his drawings for the rest of his life. He was born in Liège, the son of a printer and bookseller. From 1861 he worked as an illustrator for well-known newspapers and lived in Paris. He also designed costumes for theatres and opera houses. He is considered an early Belgian comics artist.

A hairdresser's son from Bath, Long came to London to study as a painter. He is best known for his Orientalist paintings. Many were very large. They fetched high prices. His The Babylonian Marriage Market, from 1875, is over three metres wide and perhaps his best-known work. By 1883 he had established his own selling gallery in Old Bond Street.

Mitsuoki succeeded his father, Tosa Mitsunori, as head of the Tosa school, and he brought it back to Kyoto after about fifty years in Sakai. In Sakai Mitsunori had painted for townsmen, and the school was less productive than it had been under Mitsunobu, who painted many scrolls. Mitsuoki moved to Kyoto with his father in 1634, hoping to revive the school and win back its standing at the Kyoto court. Around 1654 he gained a position as court painter, edokoro azukari. His works include Egrets and Cotton Roses.

Nuijen's father, a baker in The Hague, recognised his talent, and at twelve the boy was apprenticed to the landscape painter Andreas Schelfhout. He also studied at the Hague drawing academy under Bartholomeus Johannes van Hove. He lived only to twenty-six, but he became a prolific painter of rural and marine landscapes, spending much time on the Normandy and northern French coasts. The French Romantics influenced him greatly.

Maggiotto attended the Venice studio of Giovanni Battista Piazzetta from the age of ten and became one of his main pupils. At first he devoted himself to genre painting. In 1738 he married Elena Zuliani, and they had two sons. One of them, Francesco, became a painter and adopted his father's nickname as his own surname. His wife died in 1777. He also worked as an engraver.

Doolittle was known as the Revere of Connecticut. He became famous for four engravings of the Battles of Lexington and Concord, which were based on his first-hand reconnaissance of the battlefield. He taught himself copper engraving and also learned it through apprenticeship. His first published work in the medium appeared while he was serving in the New Haven company of the Governor's Guard. In his New Haven studio he made portraits and maps, and he also worked as a silversmith.

Löwy moved to Vienna as a boy and learned lithography, then studied painting at the Academy of Fine Arts. He opened his first studio in Vienna in 1856. In 1861 he joined the Photographische Gesellschaft, and in 1864 he took part in the first photographic exhibition in Vienna. He had a summer studio in Baden. He was an imperial and royal court photographer, as well as a publisher and industrialist.

Born Balvay in Paris, Bervic is also now known as Jean Guillaume Bervic, because of a mistake in transcribing his baptismal register. He served his first apprenticeship under Jean-Baptiste Le Prince, then left at fourteen for the studio of the engraver Jean-Georges Wille. At eighteen he won first prize for drawing at the Académie royale de peinture et de sculpture, which elected him a member in 1784. He worked mainly in intaglio and exclusively with the burin.

Very little is known about Van den Berghe. He was only rediscovered as an independent artist in the 1950s, when works formerly attributed to other artists were reattributed to him. He is believed to have been born in Antwerp, and his family left Flanders to settle in Middelburg. He may have trained under Ambrosius Bosschaert. In 1619 he registered in the Guild of St Luke in Middelburg, and in 1621 he was its dean. He signed with the monogram CvB.

Hitz became court painter to the Romanian royal family. At six she moved with her family to Ansbach, and at thirteen she was sent to Munich to study at an art school for young women, where she studied with Wilhelm von Lindenschmit the Younger. At the Art and Industrial Exhibition of 1876 she met Elisabeth of Wied, queen consort of Romania, better known by her literary name Carmen Sylva. She was a member of the November Group and a co-founder of the Berlin Secession.

Few people know the Dutch painter Murant, who painted landscapes and houses. Born in Amsterdam, he had a father who had studied in Calvinist Geneva and become a teacher. The family lived next to the school. According to Houbraken he was a pupil of Philips Wouwerman in Haarlem, where he learned to paint Italianate landscapes. He specialised in village scenes and ruined farmhouses so exact that you could count all the bricks.

Rayski is seen as a forerunner of Impressionism in Germany. He came from an aristocratic Saxon family and was born in Pegau. As a boy he studied drawing under Traugott Faber at the Freemasons' institute in Dresden, and later at the Dresden Academy of Fine Arts. He began his career as a professional artist in 1829, painting portraits. He was noted for portraits and landscapes alike.

A stonemason's son from Ferrara, Cossa is best known for his frescoes, especially the cycle of the months he painted in the Palazzo Schifanoia of the Este family, in collaboration with Cosimo Tura. After 1470 he worked in Bologna. Otherwise his paintings are mostly religious subjects, with some portraits. He also designed stained glass. Little is known about his early works.

Painter, poet and priest, Furini was a leading painter in Florence in the second quarter of the 17th century and also worked in Rome. He used a sensual sfumato style in secular and religious subjects alike, particularly in many female nudes. His father was a portrait painter who had trained under Domenico Passignano. His sister Alessandra also became a painter, and another sister, Angelica, was a singer at the court of Cosimo II.

After 1801 Giangiacomo was taught by Jean-Baptiste Wicar and commissioned to document many of the art works in Rome through engravings. He pursued this for decades and later became an instructor at the Accademia di San Luca. Among his pupils were Luigi Calamatta, Paolo Mercuri and his own son, Tertulliano. He became a member of the Congregazione de Virtuosi al Pantheon. He engraved frescoes by Pinturicchio.

Van Anthonissen painted in the style of his brother-in-law and teacher Jan Porcellis and of Jan van Goyen. Sea paintings of his in the Hermitage and the Prague Gallery were ascribed, through their signatures, to a mythical Hendrik van Antem. He lived in The Hague, Leiden and Leiderdorp in the 1630s, but from 1642 he was back in Amsterdam, where he had been born. He is known for beach scenes and seascapes.

Howard started studying with the painter Philip Reinagle in 1786, and in 1788 he began attending the Royal Academy Schools. There he won a silver medal for drawing from life and a gold medal for historical painting, for Caractacus Recognising the Dead Body of his Son. In 1791 he travelled to Italy, France and Switzerland. In Rome he met John Flaxman and John Deare and studied sculpture with them. He was a portrait and history painter.
